#6052. The Beginning of the End of Trumpism

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: The Beginning of the End of Trumpism

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Americans have now delivered on what they’ve been telling pollsters all year: They’re mad as hell and they’re not going to take it anymore. In a stunning rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, voters have entrusted Democrats with both the House and the Senate, flipping their control simultaneously for only the fourth time in a midterm election since World War II. The reverses for the GOP include defeats in usually deep-red states such as Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas.

Trump is already distancing himself from the results—after encouraging voters to pretend he was on the ballot. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform, as he cast blame on the right-wing network Fox News for platforming Democratic party voices. But polls show that voters across the country were concerned about rising costs and government corruption as they cast their ballots on Tuesday. They also show that Americans were linking their dissatisfaction over those matters directly to Trump’s policies, including the Iran war and tariffs.

Americans have now delivered on what they’ve been telling pollsters all year: They’re mad as hell and they’re not going to take it anymore. In a stunning rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, voters have entrusted Democrats with both the House and the Senate, flipping their control simultaneously for only the fourth time in a midterm election since World War II. The reverses for the GOP include defeats in usually deep-red states such as Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas.

Trump is already distancing himself from the results—after encouraging voters to pretend he was on the ballot. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform, as he cast blame on the right-wing network Fox News for platforming Democratic party voices. But polls show that voters across the country were concerned about rising costs and government corruption as they cast their ballots on Tuesday. They also show that Americans were linking their dissatisfaction over those matters directly to Trump’s policies, including the Iran war and tariffs.

Democrats should, of course, take credit for running successful campaigns in states as different as Maine, Michigan, Nevada, and North Carolina. And they ran a diverse slate of candidates, from centrists such as Adam Hamilton, a pastor who has become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since the Great Depression, to Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, one of several new House representatives associated with the Democratic Socialists of America. But that broad tent—without a clear party leader or direction—suggests that the midterm vote was more a repudiation of the present than a roadmap for the future.

It would be wise to not expect too much change immediately. “LAWYER UP,” wrote Rep. Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee and launch enquiries into the Trump administration’s actions. But Democrats will remember their failed attempts to convict and remove an already impeached Trump in his first term. Without a two-thirds majority in the House and Senate, Democrats will find that their hands remain somewhat tied in the face of a powerful executive. In case they needed a reminder, Trump already posted on Tuesday night an image of his signature red cap on Truth Social with the word “VETO” embroidered on the front in white. Yet the president will now contend with greater hurdles than he has been used to. Even if Trump restarts the Iran war or launches a new one in Cuba without congressional approval, he will face more enquires, increased public resistance, and a reduced ability to fund his pet projects.

Until Democrats coalesce around a new leader and a unifying vision, the greater checks on Trump may turn out to be systemic rather than from the Democratic Party or Congress. When it comes to waging foreign wars, whether old ones or new, the White House’s greatest restraint comes from the diminished capabilities of its defense industrial base. As is now well documented in Foreign Policy and elsewhere, the United States has expended two-thirds of its Patriot missile interceptors and one-third of its Tomahawk cruise missiles since the Iran war began. Replenishing those stockpiles could take years. Trump’s trade policies have hit repeated roadblocks in court. The president’s hold on the media—including his once-beloved Fox News, and influential right-wing commentators—has begun to slip. As I have previously written, companies and countries will see these signs of resistance and adjust how they approach Trumpworld. Entities around the world will begin to reach out to policymakers they expect to take power in two years—and this week’s results indicate they might not be Republicans. As Florida’s Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis wrote on X on Wednesday morning, the Democrats’ massive margin will take a long while to overturn. “It is very unlikely Republicans will recapture Congress in 2028,” he wrote. “Might not have a shot at Senate control until 2032.”

Beyond the partisan tug-of-war, what is clear is that the democratic system itself is holding in the face of incredible pressure. Election workers have this week ensured the integrity of democracy in the United States. Unsung state officials—both Democrats and Republicans—have fended off the Justice Department’s attempts to seize confidential voter data. Most of all, ordinary Americans, tens of millions of them buried under bills and worries, have taken the time to show that their vote counts. That is the sign of a system that is resisting historic attempts to write it off.

It is often said that the world follows the United States’ lead. Perhaps it will. It’s worth noting, however, that the U.S. midterms come amid a global mood of protest, from France to India. Countries such as Serbia and Hungary have recently booted out their leaders. And in that sense, the bigger takeaway could be that we are in a moment of historic tumult. If Trumpism was the most recognizable brand of our global moment of backlash, then perhaps we are now in the throes of a counter-backlash. Voters are realizing that the people who wanted to blow up the system—the Trumpists, if you will—don’t have the answers to our problems. Now it’s time for a sober debate about the actual solutions.

#6050. Democrats Have a Historic Opportunity to Rethink Capitalism

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Democrats Have a Historic Opportunity to Rethink Capitalism

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

“The barbarians are inside the gate,” Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson wrote on X in July in the wake of a slew of primary victories by progressive candidates. By splitting the Democratic Party and inviting the ire of Republicans, these insurgents became a defining force in the U.S. midterms, with candidates such as James Talarico and Annie Andrews winning unlikely Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina, and Peggy Flanagan and Manny Rutinel clinching victories in Minnesota and Colorado, respectively. The formal adoption of a resolution condemning socialism recently in the House of Representatives and U.S. President Donald Trump’s warnings about the “communist menace” as fundamentally un-American on the country’s 250th anniversary signal how seriously the challenge was taken this past summer, even as—amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis and growing disillusionment with the economic system—the concept of democratic socialism has become more palatable to American voters.

The verdict at the polls this week is a referendum on not just a highly consequential political contest, but also a historic battle of ideas. Having breached the gates, can this new wave of progressives change the architecture of U.S. capitalism?

“The barbarians are inside the gate,” Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson wrote on X in July in the wake of a slew of primary victories by progressive candidates. By splitting the Democratic Party and inviting the ire of Republicans, these insurgents became a defining force in the U.S. midterms, with candidates such as James Talarico and Annie Andrews winning unlikely Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina, and Peggy Flanagan and Manny Rutinel clinching victories in Minnesota and Colorado, respectively. The formal adoption of a resolution condemning socialism recently in the House of Representatives and U.S. President Donald Trump’s warnings about the “communist menace” as fundamentally un-American on the country’s 250th anniversary signal how seriously the challenge was taken this past summer, even as—amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis and growing disillusionment with the economic system—the concept of democratic socialism has become more palatable to American voters.

The verdict at the polls this week is a referendum on not just a highly consequential political contest, but also a historic battle of ideas. Having breached the gates, can this new wave of progressives change the architecture of U.S. capitalism?

On the left, politicians associated with democratic socialism, most prominently New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, have revived ideas once consigned to the margins—stronger labor institutions, higher minimum wages, universal healthcare, higher taxes, and a wider social safety net including paid family leave and government-funded preschool and college. At least 11 midterm races were decided on these issues, including the closely watched Senate race in Michigan won by Abdul El-Sayed.

But on the right, Trump, too, by introducing tariffs and returning to industrial policy, has thrown the conventional economic playbook out the window and eschewed the free-trade impulses that traditionally characterized Republican economics.

The two movements are perceived to be almost completely at odds. But what unites them is that they are—fundamentally—reactions to the economic consensus that has been dominant since the Cold War. Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who along with former U.S. President Ronald Reagan ushered in capitalism’s era of dominance, described its global embrace with the pithy phrase: “There is no alternative.”

The political scientist Francis Fukuyama subsequently coined a grand formulation to describe the alliance between free market economics and liberal democracy as an elixir of economic and political life: the “end of history.” The economic proposition that underlay it, known as neoclassical economics, proposed to replace the faltering human touch with the “invisible hand.” Built around the belief that markets could coordinate millions of strangers, it promised to convert private interest into public benefit. Without requiring shared values or common purpose, it not only relied on the rationality of the price mechanism to allocate every resource to its best use but also promised to diminish inequality.

The system succeeded in delivering global growth on an unprecedented scale, roughly tripling  the world economy in size, yet the model’s blind spots have become increasingly harder to ignore. The imperfections of the price mechanism that treats carbon as a negative externality and children a positive one, but fails to put a value on either, are becoming more glaring. Collective-action problems, such as the alignment problem presented by artificial intelligence and climate change, demonstrate that individually rational choices can produce collective outcomes that are highly irrational. And inequality has increased, particularly within countries, even as aggregate output has grown.

Most fundamentally, around the world, the human psyche is instinctively rejecting the desiccated account of human nature as solitary and narrowly self-interested, on which economics is premised, and the institutions built around these assumptions that leave people feeling increasingly alienated.

Unsurprisingly, Gallup finds that confidence in U.S. institutions is near an all-time low. In that sense, both the populist right and the progressive left are rebellions against the attempt to shoehorn humans into the role of the relentlessly utility-maximizing Homo Economicus, or Economic Man, at the heart of the narrative of economics.

Flesh-and-blood people may respond to incentives, but they equally value emotion and social connection. Yet capitalism’s scaling logic has relentlessly favored speed and size. The result has been banks that are too big to fail, “Big Tech” that concentrates power and sets off antitrust alarms, and global supply chains whose efficiency can tip rapidly into fragility. The drive for economic growth quickly outpaces the human capacity for trust.

By contrast with the proportions of most of our economic institutions, the famous Dunbar number shows that each human being can sustain roughly 150 stable relationships. At the same time, a growing body of research establishes that cooperation and reciprocity are economically salient patterns of behavior defining our relationships.

Our institutions are simultaneously too small to contend with problems on a global or planetary scale—think of climate change, artificial general intelligence, financial contagion, global poverty, and pandemics—and so are, ethically and functionally, suboptimal on a cognitive level. Yet our nation-states, domestic economies, and corporations are too large to feel affectively meaningful.

So, what if, instead of building ever-larger institutions ever faster, we built “affective institutions” that acknowledge the human capacity for fellow feeling, engage the “moral machinery” or finer feelings, and aggregate them into consensus-based communities?

Elinor Ostrom’s Nobel Prize-winning scholarship illustrates, through examples such as forests, fisheries, and irrigation systems around the world, that community governance structures can rival markets and governments by deploying locally constructed norms to create robust economic communities.

Her findings are often considered quaint because of the constraint on institutional size that they impose, but new breakthroughs in network science provide a possible answer to the problem of scale. Dense communities where reputation and repeated interaction matter can be linked through threads or bridges that connect those communities, allowing information, capital, and successful practices to travel between them. The resulting architecture is a latticework of fishnets connected through fireworks, a system that is cohesive but not centralized, balancing local trust and large-scale reach.

Real-world models of what these “affective institutions” might look like already exist. Mondragon’s cooperatives in the Basque region of Spain combine locally governed, largely autonomous enterprises embedded in a shared financial structure. The group employed more than 71,000 people and recorded more than $12 billion in sales in 2025, serving as a significant proof of concept.

The 27-country-strong European Union, whose membership includes previously warring nations, represents a much larger, more ambitious experiment. Indeed, its structure, based on the principle of subsidiarity—which holds that decisions should remain at national, regional, or local level unless they can be achieved more effectively at the EU level because of their scale or effects—suggests a more useful economic approach than whether government should be bigger or smaller: At what level should each problem be solved, and how should those levels connect?

This new blueprint is of direct relevance to progressives across the United States. After America’s socialist summer, the question is whether the collective effervescence of the movement can congeal into something that can be sustained.

If the “warmth of collectivism” spreading from New York’s experiment with Zohranomics is to spark a revolution that tackles not just the crisis of affordability but also human agency, then the right scaling technology, built around citizens, consensus, and resilience, will be key. The midterms present a historic opportunity to turn widespread voter disaffection away from the self-destructive nihilism of the Make America Great Again movement and toward constructive agency. That will require moving beyond the stale market-versus-state binary and building structures rooted in individuals, embedded in communities, and linked through diffuse but connected networks. The scientific breakthrough has already happened; the politics just needs to catch up.

Few projects could be more faithful to the American promise than putting people—and the relationships between them—back at the center of economic and social life. Progressives now have a chance to stop being cast as the “barbarians at the gate” and storm the political citadel instead. But to do that, they will need to remodel the architecture of U.S. capitalism, by human hand.

They should reclaim key parts of Joe Biden’s record, rather than run from it.

Antara Haldar is an associate professor at the University of Cambridge and the author of Everyman: The Untold Story of Economics.

#6047. U.S. Democracy Is Back—Sort of

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: U.S. Democracy Is Back—Sort of

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The message of the 2026 midterm elections is decidedly in: U.S. democracy is not dead, not by a long shot.

There is, at long last, the glimmer of a beginning to the end of President Donald Trump’s decade-long dominance of national politics. Most of all, the 2028 presidential race—which effectively begins today—is now up in the air. So is the ultimate direction of the country’s international role, which will be decided by that election.

The message of the 2026 midterm elections is decidedly in: U.S. democracy is not dead, not by a long shot.

There is, at long last, the glimmer of a beginning to the end of President Donald Trump’s decade-long dominance of national politics. Most of all, the 2028 presidential race—which effectively begins today—is now up in the air. So is the ultimate direction of the country’s international role, which will be decided by that election.

But no one should kid themselves that the next two years are going to be anything other than ugly, chaotic, and brutal. Both Democrats and Republicans will be engaged in vicious infighting over fundamental policy issues, whether the question is the survival of the international order, engagement with allies and adversaries alike, immigration policy, or tariffs and the strength of the economy.

Above all, it’s important to note that even with the dramatic turnover in Congress—with Democrats taking back both the House and Senate in decisive fashion—the president has shown very little inclination to defer to Congress, or even to the courts, on any issue that involves foreign or domestic policy.

That Trumpian defiance will continue, whether the question is finding a way to end his prolonged Iran war on palatable terms, force a resolution to Russia’s nearly five-year-long invasion of Ukraine, persist in his crackdown on immigrants, or continue to unilaterally impose tariffs on whomever he pleases. In an Election Day interview with CBS News, Trump declared that even if the Democrats take control, he is prepared to use “tremendous” executive power to push through his agenda. “I have the ultimate power—it’s called ‘veto,’” he said.

Trump also has the power of the executive order. In less than two years, he has signed 292 executive orders, 90 memoranda, and 192 proclamations, touching critical policies from voting rights to the reversal of 80 years of trade policy.

But facts are a stubborn thing. In his second term, the economic news was so grim and Trump’s abuse of power so brazen—he pushed the Justice Department to prosecute his enemies, enriched his family, and launched a costly war with no legal basis—that even many of those voters who supported him two years ago could no longer look away. In the weeks leading up to the vote, Trump’s approval ratings fell to historic lows. The result was an equally historic rebuke, one so profound that even deeply red states turned against Trump. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico won the Senate race and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa was elected as the first Democratic governor in 32 years. Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas in 94 years.

“The system is working,” said Charles Kupchan of the Council on Foreign Relations, author of the new book, Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come. “Voters have held accountable a president who has been failing to deliver on virtually all fronts.”

But Kupchan added: “Democratic control of Congress will have virtually no impact on Trump’s foreign policy. He has largely disregarded the preferences of the legislature on matters of statecraft—and will certainly continue to do so with Congress in the hands of Democrats.  On domestic policy, expect confrontation, paralysis, and a swirl of investigations.”

Still, it’s clear that as a political force, Trump is badly damaged—no doubt permanently as he finishes out his last term at the age of 80. The president brazenly made the midterm election a referendum about himself. “Pretend I’m on the ballot,” he said frequently in the weeks before the election. Following Tuesday’s devastating vote, however, the rebuffed president reversed course. He suggested the problem was not him but the flawed candidates the GOP put forward, including the corruption-plagued Ken Paxton in Texas (whom Trump had endorsed in the primary) and the  fumbling Darline Graham in South Carolina (whom Trump had recommended). Both went down to defeat.

“I wasn’t on the ballot and, if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE,” Trump posted on Truth Social late Tuesday night as the Republican defeat took shape.

Republicans successfully connected wartime spending to the rising price of pork chops.

The president’s hold on national politics finally gave way Tuesday.

Trump also backed away from threats of declaring voter fraud the way he did after his 2020 defeat in the presidential election, telling the New York Times that he is “absolutely willing” to accept the results. Of Democrats, he said, “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”

Trump is clearly concerned about his legacy. Now he and his GOP successors will have to address the fracturing of the MAGA coalition that returned Trump to the White House in 2024.

And following Tuesday’s election, it’s fair to say that that coalition no longer exists.

In 2024, Trump exploited an inflationary environment under President Joe Biden and the seeming takeover of the Democratic Party by progressive, so-called woke issues—not to mention a degree of misogyny and racism directed at Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic candidate—to win over formerly Democratic leaning blue-collar voters, especially Latino and Black men. Together with his neo-isolationist MAGA base, that was enough to put him over the edge against Harris.

But earlier this year, Trump inflicted a catastrophic double wound on himself by launching an ill-justified war against Iran. In doing so he simultaneously alienated many middle-income voters who have been hammered by rising prices spiked by the war—as well as disenchanted MAGA voters who feel betrayed over his previous promises to avoid foreign wars and restore the economy.

Many Latino voters who went heavily Democratic in Tuesday’s election also appeared to be alienated by Trump’s broad crackdown on immigrants, especially since the dragnet has pulled in some legal residents.

Trump was rebuffed across the board by many of these voters. As Politico’s Playbook noted, “The cross-country transformation of the Latino voting electorate will go down as one of the biggest stories of the night. From a full sweep in Texas’ Mexican-American Rio Grande Valley to Pennsylvania’s Puerto Rican-dominated Lehigh Valley to even Dem gains in heavily Puerto Rican, Cuban, Venezuelan and Colombian central and south Florida, all showed the same direction toward Democrats.”

Looking ahead to 2028, many of those newly alienated former Trump voters will be up for grabs. The question is whether a badly divided Democratic Party will be in a position to draw them in.

“The biggest challenge for Democrats will be to unite around a platform focused on health insurance, housing, and industrial policies geared to fostering inclusive growth, labor-market transformation for the AI economy, and assistance for those who will bear the costs of the transition,” said Ian Shapiro, a political scientist at Yale University. “They should pass bill after bill on these issues, even if Trump vetoes them all. They will become the basis for their Project 2029, which serious contenders for the Democratic presidential nomination will have to embrace.”

And yet the Democrats show little sign of doing that. The new slate in the House and Senate consists of a large ideological spread of legislators ranging from moderates to left-wing populists who are aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. Prominent among them: the senator-elect from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate. And before it settles on a 2028 nominee, the party will be engulfed in big fights over taxes, healthcare, and foreign policy, especially support for Israel.

#6044. Where Democrats Can Thwart Trump’s Foreign Policy

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: Where Democrats Can Thwart Trump’s Foreign Policy

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

U.S. President Donald Trump has wielded the powers of the presidency like a sledgehammer during his second term—especially in foreign policy—and frequently bypassed Congress. From launching the Iran war and ordering strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats near Latin America, to the operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Trump has repeatedly taken major military action without congressional approval.

With Republicans controlling Congress in Trump’s second term so far, Democrats have been extremely limited in their capacity to challenge the White House on this and many other fronts. But that’s about to change. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with stunning upsets in races nationwide. This opens the door for Democrats to steer the United States in new directions on a range of key foreign policy issues after the new Congress is sworn in early next year.

U.S. President Donald Trump has wielded the powers of the presidency like a sledgehammer during his second term—especially in foreign policy—and frequently bypassed Congress. From launching the Iran war and ordering strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats near Latin America, to the operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Trump has repeatedly taken major military action without congressional approval.

With Republicans controlling Congress in Trump’s second term so far, Democrats have been extremely limited in their capacity to challenge the White House on this and many other fronts. But that’s about to change. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with stunning upsets in races nationwide. This opens the door for Democrats to steer the United States in new directions on a range of key foreign policy issues after the new Congress is sworn in early next year.

Democrats will have control over the appropriations committees in both chambers and oversee the drafting of annual military and foreign aid spending bills. This far from guarantees that Democrats will get their way, but the power of the purse will grant them considerable influence and negotiating power. Ahead of the midterms, top Democrats in Congress said that they would move to cut funding for the Iran war if they regained power. Now, a Democratic-controlled Congress will be able to leverage funding and make good on this pledge.

“Attaching a funding prohibition to a must-pass piece of funding legislation” would be the most effective “mechanism for forcing an end” to either the Iran war or boat strikes, Brian Finucane, a senior advisor at the International Crisis Group and a former attorney advisor at the State Department, told Foreign Policy.

As a potential model to follow, Finucane pointed to the example of Congress nearly forcing a government shutdown in 1973 to end then-President Richard Nixon’s bombing of Cambodia. If they’re willing to “play hardball” in this fashion and have the “political will,” then Democrats in the new Congress could probably “shut down” both the Iran war and the “lawless boat strikes,” he said. Experts have emphasized that the strikes on the alleged drug boats are illegal under both domestic and international law—an assessment that’s shared by leading congressional Democrats.

Democrats will also be taking control of Congress amid an evolving debate in Washington over what the next chapter of U.S. engagement in the Middle East should look like, fostered in part by the significant damage that U.S. bases in the Gulf have sustained amid the Iran war.

“Our bases there are going to need to be rebuilt or moved elsewhere. They’ve been heavily hit by Iran. That’s an appropriations issue 101,” Joshua Shifrinson, a professor at the University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy and an international security expert, said. Democrats will be able to “move the needle” on the issue of the U.S. presence in the Middle East by virtue of the fact that decisions will have to be made over whether to direct funding to rebuilding damaged installations or moving them elsewhere, Shifrinson added.

Similarly, the appropriations process will also make the needle movable when it comes to the future of the U.S. presence in Europe and its policy toward Ukraine, Shifrinson said. Democrats have fervently opposed Trump administration plans to reduce the U.S. military footprint in Europe, and have expressed outrage over the White House’s lack of support for Kyiv and recent efforts to reduce economic penalties for Moscow amid the Russia-Ukraine war. Much like Iran and the boat strikes, congressional Democrats are likely to use funding as a bargaining chip to challenge Trump on both issues. Democrats also signaled that regaining a majority would help speed up the passage of new aid packages for Ukraine, which have historically garnered bipartisan support.

The new Congress will still face significant constraints in its ability to counter Trump, and he’s vowed to charge ahead with his agenda regardless of the results. Trump is likely to continue leaning heavily on executive orders—which he’s done even as Republicans have controlled Congress—and has said he’ll veto Democratic legislation that he opposes. Given the immense political divide in the United States at present, Democrats will be unlikely to have the necessary support from Republicans to override Trump’s veto, which requires a two-thirds supermajority vote in both the House and Senate.

The president’s hold on national politics finally gave way Tuesday.

What the mass disapproval of U.S. voters means for the world.

Despite such challenges, there are still other ways the incoming Democratic Congress can shape U.S. foreign policy beyond appropriations or legislation. Oversight is poised to play a particularly big role in how Democrats could shape U.S. foreign policy moving forward. Thanks to their big wins on Tuesday, Democrats will soon control powerful congressional committees with the ability to launch investigations, convene hearings, and issue subpoenas.

Democrats “can and should” use the “investigative powers of controlling committees to call hearings on any number of issues, ranging from Iran war oversight to foreign influence over U.S. policy, which would include corruption by the Trump family or potentially illicit foreign dealings,” Shifrinson said. “High-level investigations of all these facets of foreign policy … are very likely going forward.”

Trump has faced allegations from Democrats of using the power of his office to facilitate deals with foreign governments that are advantageous to his family and their business interests. This is likely to be a “substantial theme for oversight in the House and potentially in the Senate,” Finucane said. Democrats have already “not so subtly” indicated “that this is coming down the road” with letters to the administration. The administration’s “various dealings with Venezuela, including the oil sector,” are poised to be a topic of particularly aggressive oversight by congressional Democrats, he added.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is now set to become chair of the House Oversight Committee, has pledged to investigate the Trump family for alleged crimes. On Tuesday night, he issued a blunt warning: “Lawyer up.”

Additionally, Senate Democrats could use their majority to block or delay national security nominees that they consider unfit for their prospective roles or as a means of bringing the Trump administration to the negotiation table on other issues.

There are also indications that Democrats will use their new oversight authorities to pursue impeachment proceedings against administration officials, with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the top of the list of possible targets. Democrats have been adamant that they want more answers on the decisions and failures surrounding the Iran war. Holding hearings on the war will put an uncomfortable spotlight on the administration—and the Republican Party more generally—and could tee up Democrats to keep using Iran as a line of political attack in the leadup to the 2028 presidential election.

There’s also the possibility that Democrats will be able to bring at least some Republicans in Congress to their side on foreign policy issues like the Iran war, given its undeniable influence on the midterm results. Trump himself conceded that the Iran war was a “piece” of why the GOP lost. Meanwhile, Democrats could use their new authority in Congress to push for legislative reforms that would aim to prevent future presidents from taking foreign-policy actions similar to Trump’s. Such efforts would likely be vetoed, but they could help set the stage for important changes under later administrations.

“We’re really at a generational high point in terms of the political salience of these war powers issues, because Americans can feel the consequences of the president going to war lawlessly,” Finucane said. The 1973 War Powers Resolution “unfortunately failed to stop Trump from embarking upon this military misadventure” with Iran, he added, and Democrats “need to start laying the groundwork for structural reform to prevent further such a catastrophe.”

#6042. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel’s Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

#6041. Trump’s Next Trade War Could Be With Congress

Analysis: Trump’s Next Trade War Could Be With Congress

Dissatisfaction with U.S. President Donald Trump’s disastrous, expensive, and self-defeating trade policies were a big reason for the sweeping Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections—and may turn tariffs and trade into one of the crucial battlegrounds of the next Congress.

Concern over the economy was far and away the most pressing issue for voters, according to exit polls, and those concerns were mainly about inflation and stubbornly high prices. While higher energy prices were caused in part (as Trump acknowledged) by the war in Iran, Trump’s tariffs on friends and foes alike have for two years raised costs for businesses and consumers. Overall, about two-thirds of all voters said Trump’s tariffs had hurt them economically, with the pain sharpest among Democratic voters.

Dissatisfaction with U.S. President Donald Trump’s disastrous, expensive, and self-defeating trade policies were a big reason for the sweeping Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections—and may turn tariffs and trade into one of the crucial battlegrounds of the next Congress.

Concern over the economy was far and away the most pressing issue for voters, according to exit polls, and those concerns were mainly about inflation and stubbornly high prices. While higher energy prices were caused in part (as Trump acknowledged) by the war in Iran, Trump’s tariffs on friends and foes alike have for two years raised costs for businesses and consumers. Overall, about two-thirds of all voters said Trump’s tariffs had hurt them economically, with the pain sharpest among Democratic voters.

What’s more, it’s not just a rejection of tariffs, erroneously sold by Trump as a tax on foreigners, but a broad-based rejection of the notion that one man and his whims can hijack American wallets. According to one September poll, 70 percent of Americans believe that the president should seek congressional approval before levying new tariffs.

Now, with a large and unassailable majority in both chambers, and with ever fewer Republicans bound in fealty to a lame-duck president, lawmakers have a real chance to claw back the constitutional power over trade and taxation that they have dribbled away over the last century. And Trump himself has suggested that he does not want to spend his last two years of relevance “vetoing everything,” which opens the door to congressional fixes that could actually become law. Rep. Richard Neal, the ranking member and soon-to-be-again chair of the House Ways and Means Committee—the main conduit for trade legislation—indicated the tenor of the incoming Congress in his fulminations this fall against the latest Russian sanctions bill, which controversially gave Trump even more power to use tariffs. (Trump embraced the tariffs but waived the sanctions on Russia.)

“This bill is a tariff tyrant’s fantasy come true,” Neal said in a September speech. “Congress has a job to do. Do it. Don’t give it away.”

Congress tried earlier in Trump’s second term, with timid efforts, to restrain the president’s power to unilaterally raise taxes on Americans. None of those congressional efforts bore fruit, but that was a different Congress.

“The Americans have spoken: Affordability is a major issue, and that is tied into tariffs, which are very unpopular,” said Alan Wolff, a former U.S. Treasury Department official who has worked on trade issues since the Nixon administration.

“Among those who look at trade statutes, these conversations are becoming quite lively right now,” added Wolff, who is now at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

With Congress in Democratic hands starting early next year, Trump’s bullying tactics on trade may face a check that could embolden victimized countries to take a page out of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s playbook and push back against the U.S. executive branch’s abuse of its delegated authorities.

But the real action may come on the domestic front.

There are actions Congress could take even during the lame-duck session, before most of the new lawmakers take their seats in January. Trump’s trade war with Canada, for instance, is wildly unpopular in border states and is predicated on the flimsiest of foundations. (Those tariffs, like all his others, are currently being litigated.)

“As far as I know, there is zero sentiment in Congress, on either side of the aisle, for the Section 338 tariffs” used against Canada, Wolff said. “That could be one place you could pick up some Republican votes even during the lame duck.”

The court challenge to that latest Trump tariff has two arguments. One is that the 1930 statute Trump invoked, for the first time ever, has been overtaken and superseded by subsequent trade legislation in the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s. It’s a valid argument, backed by Supreme Court precedent, but it’s nebulous.

Congress could quash the debate entirely.

“They could explicitly say that Sec. 338 has been superseded,” Wolff said.

Looking ahead, that strategy—making trade law more explicit, with an eye to making judicial review easier—may be the clearest path forward for Congress. Trump has already been dealt several court defeats on his tariffs, but if Congress weighed in to clarify what trade powers have been delegated and under what conditions, it would make the courts’ job easier.

Two additional statutes could be in the crosshairs. Section 232 of the 1962 Trade Expansion Act allows the president to slap tariffs on imports on national security grounds. That has been a favorite of Trump’s since his first term; in his second, he has expanded national security concerns to include bathroom fittings and lumber. Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act allows the president to take targeted action against individual countries that discriminate against U.S. commerce; Trump used it against nearly every U.S. trading partner, on the grounds that they don’t adequately enforce laws against the use of slave labor. (That, too, is currently in court.)

One simple fix, suggested Simon Lester, a trade lawyer, would be to amend those statutes so that they would comply with international trade law. That would require any tariffs under those statutes to comply with World Trade Organization rules, which they currently don’t. Such measures, he argued, would make it easier for courts to see what are valid uses of presidential trade authority and what are abuses.

Of course, the tug of war between Congress and the executive branch has gone on for at least a century. The reason that Congress began delegating trade authority to the White House, which culminated in Trump’s impulsive reign of trade terror, was because Congress made such a hash of tariff policy in the 1930 Smoot-Hawley bill—the very thing that Trump leaned on for his Canada tariffs.

The issue for the next Congress is how far to let the pendulum swing.

“The Sec. 301 actions and Sec. 232 actions—that is low-hanging fruit,” Wolff said. “The question is how far they want to go without having a close look at all the trade authorities and see where they went wrong.”

Wolff was in the trenches for the last big comprehensive trade overhaul that sought to balance the president’s need to have some power over tariffs and trade (for foreign-policy purposes) and Congress’s right to oversee taxation. That was the 1974 Trade Act. But that took two years. So it is unlikely that, Trump’s veto pen aside, the next Congress will be able to entirely rebalance the trade relationship back toward constitutional equilibrium.

It should, though. Much as the undeclared Iran war hovered over the minds of midterm voters, congressional abdication on trade did as well. Both stem from the same root, and both have the same solution.

“A declaration of war requires an act of Congress,” Wolff said. “So why shouldn’t the declaration of a trade war?”

#6039. DeSantis nukes ‘tech guy’ Vivek after Ohio drubbing: ‘Not in tune’ with blue-collar voters

Vivek Ramaswamy addressed supporters at GOP headquarters in Columbus after the gubernatorial race was called for Democrat Amy Acton.

Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis blasted failed Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and his GOP handlers, arguing on a podcast that he wasn't "in tune" with the working-class people of the state.

Biotech entrepreneur Ramaswamy lost his scandal-plagued race to Democratic candidate Amy Acton by 7.9 percentage points. Despite President Donald Trump’s endorsement and guidance from Vice President JD Vance’s top advisers, Ramaswamy lost amid a "blue wave" that produced major Democratic upsets across the country. The midterm elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's presidency.

But DeSantis, who ran for president in 2024 and is term-limited after 2026, shared on the Sage Steele Show that Ramaswamy bore some responsibility for his loss.

"I don't know why they would have pushed him to be the candidate there. Oh, my mom's from Youngstown. Ohio is a working class state, very blue collar. You know Vivek, he's like a tech guy," DeSantis said.

RAMASWAMY OUTLINES KEY CONTRASTS WITH DEM OPPONENT LESS THAN 100 DAYS OUT FROM KEY GUBERNATORIAL ELECTION

Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks during a campaign rally on February 25, 2025, at the Glass City Center in Toledo, Ohio. (Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Ramaswamy, who previously ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024, is the founder of biotech company Roivant Sciences and anti-ESG investment firm Strive Asset Management. He also briefly co-led President Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency with Elon Musk.

He was warmly embraced by Trump, who endorsed him the same day Ramaswamy announced his candidacy. Trump had previously encouraged Ramaswamy to consider seeking Vance’s former Senate seat. Ramaswamy and Vance have known each other since their time at Yale Law School.

DeSantis criticized Ramaswamy’s support for a merit-based H-1B visa system, arguing that it likely further distanced him from Ohio’s blue-collar voters. Ramaswamy had said the current lottery-based system should be "gutted."

'He wants to bring in foreign workers on visas. That is not the type of person that's going to sell." DeSantis said.

Ramaswamy's own companies have used the H-1B program, with Roivant Sciences having 29 H-1B applications approved between 2018 and 2023.

Meanwhile, Strive Asset Management, the investment firm he co-founded, moved its headquarters from Columbus to Dallas in 2025, months before Ramaswamy launched his campaign for Ohio governor. Ramaswamy said he was no longer involved in the company’s operations, but remained a major shareholder.

"And I know he shot himself in the foot," DeSantis said. "I know he did a lot of other stuff to make it a real landslide against him. "I think we would have done better in Ohio had we had a candidate that was more representative or more in tune with the interests of kind of these blue collar people that make the backbone of Ohio."

Just weeks before the election, Ramaswamy’s campaign drew bipartisan outrage for using Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton’s estranged mother in an attack ad that called the Democratic candidate a "liar" and disputed her account of childhood poverty and homelessness.

The ad omitted that Acton had not seen or spoken to her mother since age 12, when her stepfather was arrested on charges of raping her. He pleaded not guilty but fled the area before trial, and court records show authorities continued seeking his arrest for years. Acton’s brother has said their mother remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Ramaswamy's loss, alongside Republican U.S. Senate candidate Jon Husted's loss to Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown by 4.9 percentage points, came just two years after Trump won the state by 11.2 percentage points.

In addition to criticizing Ramaswamy, DeSantis took aim at Congress, saying Republicans are now on the "defensive" and faulting lawmakers for failing to codify Trump’s executive orders into law.

"Last night's elections did not only kneecap the last two years of the Trump administration, it basically ensures the four years after that are going to either be Democrat years where they have a trifecta or where you have a Republican president that is hemmed in and limited," DeSantis said.

DeSantis also pushed back against any 2028 speculation.

"The only way that I would run for any office is if you can actually deliver big results," DeSantis said. "I don't want to just be a timepiece where I just sit there like a potted plant."

#6038. At the Races: After the deluge

By Mary Ellen McIntire, Daniela Altimari and Niels Lesniewski

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they’ve so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That’s how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

Dispatch: For Ukrainians, U.S. Midterm Results Bring Some Hope

Understanding the conflict four years in.

KYIV AND WASHINGTON—The outcome of the U.S. congressional elections this week, which gave Democrats control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, will be welcomed in some countries more than others, including Ukraine—which has quarreled with Republican-controlled Washington off and on for two years now.

So what are ordinary Ukrainians saying about the results?

KYIV AND WASHINGTON—The outcome of the U.S. congressional elections this week, which gave Democrats control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, will be welcomed in some countries more than others, including Ukraine—which has quarreled with Republican-controlled Washington off and on for two years now.

So what are ordinary Ukrainians saying about the results?

In Kyiv, which is now preparing for a brutal winter, some residents seemed cautiously optimistic. But on a day marked by sweeping power and water cuts following a barrage of Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, Ukrainians appeared far more focused on ensuring their daily survival.

“The main thing for us is that there’s water and electricity—and no war,” said Yulia, who declined to give her last name. “I hope things will be better.”

The U.S. midterm results come as Russia has ramped up its campaign of hybrid warfare in Europe and escalated its attacks against Ukraine, damaging critical infrastructure and regularly upending daily life across the country. In Kyiv on Wednesday, disruptions to energy and water supplies prompted officials to establish emergency centers in hard-hit areas and urge residents to get their water from public fountains.

Those impacts were visible at one café in the city, which was forced to rely on a generator for power. A staff member told Foreign Policy that the generator had already been running for eight hours. Elsewhere in the café, a row of power packs for rent testified to the difficulty of doing much without electricity.

Maxim Yersigngeyev, who had brought his young daughter to have breakfast at the café due to a blackout at home, said he didn’t particularly follow the U.S. election. “But if it’s good for Ukraine, that’s good,” he said.

In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, search-and-rescue operations have been underway after Russian forces bombed a humanitarian hub on Monday, killing at least 40 people and leaving dozens more missing under the rubble. The attack could rank among one of the deadliest against civilians in nearly five years of war.

The timing of that strike, as well as other Russian strikes earlier this week, drew a sharp response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said that it was “very telling” that the attacks coincided with the U.S. congressional elections.

“The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelensky said in a post on X on Tuesday. “It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that.”

Tensions have been high between Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump, with one sticking point being the powerful Patriot air defense interceptors that can shield against Russian ballistic missile attacks.

Zelensky has warned of shrinking supplies of the weapons and accused the United States of slow-rolling deliveries, and the Trump administration has previously backtracked on pledges to share the technology underpinning the missiles with Kyiv.

The Trump administration last week approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of the missiles for Ukraine, although Zelensky has said that it could take “several years” for the weapons to arrive. The sale runs through a U.S. program and would be completely funded by Canada, Norway, and Germany.

And further negotiations are on the horizon. On Wednesday, the European Commission is set to host representatives from Ukraine, the United States, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, NATO, and the World Bank for talks on postwar reconstruction and security guarantees.

Next week, Washington is also expected to mediate talks between Kyiv and Moscow in Abu Dhabi, with discussions focusing on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace,” U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff announced in a post on X.

Back in Kyiv, Valeriy Shevchenko told Foreign Policy that he was happy with the Democrats’ wins but had his eye more on the 2028 presidential election.

“But as you see, we are constantly being attacked, specifically through power outages—we need to rely on ourselves,” he said, referring to Ukrainian air defenses.

#6034. Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Midterms Wipeout

U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance on Wednesday offered an extraordinarily frank assessment of why he believes Republicans got clobbered in the 2026 midterm elections. He blamed the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on X.

U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance on Wednesday offered an extraordinarily frank assessment of why he believes Republicans got clobbered in the 2026 midterm elections. He blamed the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on X.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance added. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

It’s not often that a sitting vice president comes out so forcefully against a defining policy decision made by his boss—especially when that boss is as notorious for punishing perceived disloyalty as U.S. President Donald Trump is.

But Vance, who is widely expected to be interested in running for president in 2028, appears to have calculated that the political cost of continuing to defend the Iran war outweighs the potential risk of drawing Trump’s ire.

In the lead-up to elections, polling consistently showed that the Iran war was unpopular among voters and that the cost of living was their top concern.

As Vance noted, Trump himself has acknowledged that the Iran war was a “piece” of what contributed to the historic defeat. But the president remains unapologetic about starting the war.

“I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal.

Trump also blamed the quality of Republican candidates on the ballot, stating that some could’ve been “better.” In a separate interview with Fox News, Trump acknowledged voter discontentment over the war’s economic consequences, including high gas prices, but suggested the pain at the pump was worth it in the long run.

“People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really, probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline,” Trump said. “And, you know, I understand that. I don’t agree with it, and I would say to people, you know, ‘It’s a short-term problem but for long-term gain.’”

But Trump and Vance have never done a particularly good job of selling the Iran war to the American people. Since the very beginning, the administration has presented muddled and often contradictory explanations for why the United States needed to launch a full-scale war on Iran in February.

Even in his final speech on the eve of the election, Trump undermined the war’s main justification by saying that Iran’s nuclear program had already been destroyed by U.S. military action last summer.

“I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon. If, if we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way. The whole world would be a different place, so we’ve stopped that. We stopped that a year ago with those beautiful B-2 bombers, which hit every single mark, and just put hundreds of tons of rock on top of everything,” Trump said.

Vance is believed to have strongly opposed the war behind closed doors; yet he outwardly maintained support for it. It seems that American voters’ unequivocal rejection of the war has convinced him that he no longer has to pretend.

John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger

#6032. Democrats Won Big in the U.S. Midterms. What’s Next?

World Brief: Democrats Won Big in the U.S. Midterms. What’s Next?
